title: IntersectionObserver
learningObjectives: Explain intersectionobserver and use the browser API with appropriate lifecycle and privacy safeguards.

understand.concept: IntersectionObserver asynchronously reports when a target intersects a root or viewport. It is commonly used for lazy loading, visibility tracking, and infinite-scroll sentinels. Observers should be disconnected when no longer needed.
understand.whyItMatters: It avoids repeated scroll calculations and lets the browser optimise intersection detection. It is not an exact pixel-by-pixel scroll event replacement.
understand.analogy: An observer is a lookout that reports when an item enters or leaves a defined viewing area.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; browser API support, permission, lifecycle, and security rules vary by platform.

explain.narrative: The callback reports intersection changes; each target is unobserved after it becomes visible.

examples.explanation: The callback reports intersection changes; each target is unobserved after it becomes visible.
examples.expectedOutput: Browser console or UI output demonstrates the API; permission and secure-context features require a supported environment.

practise.guidedTask: Lazy-load a non-critical image when its container enters the viewport. Disconnect or unobserve targets after use.
practise.independentTask: Build a small feature using the API. Include feature detection, permission or failure handling, cleanup, and an accessible alternative where relevant.
hints: Do not assume the API is available in every browser.
Request sensitive permissions only after explaining why.
Clean up observers, workers, and listeners when no longer needed.

questions.prompt: Which API is designed to observe when an element intersects a root or viewport?
What is a reliable approach when using browser APIs?
options: Feature-detect, handle denial or failure, and clean up resources
questions.answer: Feature-detect, handle denial or failure, and clean up resources
questions.explanation: Browser features need graceful fallback, privacy-aware permission, and lifecycle management.
